lore.story:
Lewis Carroll invented the ultimate flex: a cat so confident it could vanish completely and leave just the smile behind, main-character energy made visible.

The phrase "grin like a Cheshire cat" was already floating around English slang before Carroll ever picked up a pen in 1865, and nobody's fully sure why.
lore.didYouKnow: That crescent-moon brooch is basically a spoiler: legend has it the Cat disappears tail-first, saving the grin for last — the OG mic-drop exit.
lore.historicalCaption: John Tenniel's original 1865 illustration — the exact grin that started the saying.
lore.loadingFact: In the original 1865 illustrations, the Cheshire Cat is drawn with stripes — the wide, toothy grin as we picture it today mostly came later, from stage and film.

lore.story:
A miller's youngest son inherited nothing but a cat and figured he'd gotten scammed.

The cat had other plans — bluffing an ogre, flattering a king, and turning his broke owner into a marquis, one increasingly ridiculous lie at a time.
lore.didYouKnow: That tiny gold boot charm swinging from the belt is literally the accessory that gave this cat his name — and his powers of persuasion.
lore.historicalCaption: Gustave Doré's 19th-century engraving of the original scheming cat.
lore.loadingFact: In some versions of the tale, the miller's son never gets a name at all — just an ever-growing list of titles his cat invented for him.

lore.story:
Le Chat Noir wasn't just a cat, it was Paris's entire nightlife scene wearing a mascot costume. The Montmartre cabaret opened in 1881 and became ground zero for poets, painters, and shockingly literal shadow-puppet shows.

Its 1896 poster — a black cat arched under a gold halo — became one of the most bootlegged images in art history.
lore.didYouKnow: The glowing sunburst embroidered behind the cat recreates that exact poster almost line for line.
lore.historicalCaption: The real 1896 poster — still one of art history's most bootlegged images.
lore.loadingFact: The cabaret's founder styled himself a mock-nobleman and signed letters 'Lord of Chat Noir' — the cat outranked him by the end.

lore.story:
Freyja, Norse goddess of love, beauty, and war, did not do horses. She had two enormous grey cats haul her chariot instead, because apparently even goddesses have main-character pet preferences.

Norwegian folklore later insisted that feeding a stray cat well was basically a direct line to Freyja's good graces.
lore.didYouKnow: The amber beads draped across the collar are a real nod to Viking-age jewelry — amber was one of Scandinavia's most valuable trade goods, and Freyja herself was said to weep tears of gold.
lore.historicalCaption: Freyja mid-flight, cat-drawn chariot and all.
lore.loadingFact: Domestic cats barely existed in Scandinavia when the earliest Freyja myths were told — some scholars think the original 'cats' were actually lynxes.

lore.story:
No cat had been to space before Félicette. None has gone since.

France strapped a calm Parisian stray into a rocket, wired her up to monitor her brain activity in zero gravity, and sent her past the edge of the atmosphere. Minutes later her capsule parachuted safely back down, making her the only cat ever confirmed to survive spaceflight.
lore.didYouKnow: The tiny satellite and star charms on this dress mark a flight that lasted just minutes but made Félicette the answer to a very specific trivia question, forever.
lore.historicalCaption: The real Félicette, photographed right after her 1963 flight.
lore.loadingFact: A male cat was originally slated for the flight and reportedly bolted right before launch — Félicette got the job instead.
